frictionVectors.title: European Gas Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons through Sonatrach while Europe seeks dependable gas supplies and greater investment access. Price volatility and infrastructure requirements constrain fiscal flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and the wider Sahel increases security costs around energy corridors and border regions. Algiers is resisting deeper foreign military involvement while expanding regional diplomatic influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains heavily dependent on offshore oil revenue, with production constraints and debt-service obligations limiting sovereign policy space. Chinese financing remains important even as Luanda diversifies toward Western and Gulf partners.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The United States and European partners are backing the Lobito Corridor to access critical minerals from the Copperbelt. The project offers infrastructure gains but may deepen competition over transport rents, mineral access, and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Trade Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over border access, sanctions legacies, and the operation of oil-export infrastructure through Benin. Disruption threatens port revenues and regional trade connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity from the Sahel is increasing pressure on Benin's northern frontier and transport routes. International security assistance supports capacity but risks creating dependence on external intelligence and financing.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with De Beers and is demanding greater local value capture from diamonds. The country still faces exposure to global diamond demand and the commercial power of international firms.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and Water Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and other mineral projects require external capital, rail links, and reliable water and power supplies. Gaborone is seeking diversification without sacrificing regulatory control or environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Sovereignty Push
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening control over gold production, licensing, and refining to capture more state revenue and reduce foreign-company dominance. Weak administrative capacity and insecurity complicate enforcement and raise investment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is deepening security cooperation with Russia while reducing reliance on France and regional institutions. This provides political autonomy but increases exposure to opaque security arrangements, sanctions risk, and civilian-protection concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border interference continue to constrain trade, security cooperation, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and informal networks remain important in gold and mineral production, while limited electricity infrastructure weakens domestic value capture.

highlights: Atlantic gateway with strong institutional control
Renewables and maritime security are strategic priorities

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, remittances, development finance, and foreign investment underpin the economy, leaving infrastructure and fiscal policy exposed to outside shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: The islands' location attracts security, port, and logistics partnerships, requiring careful balancing among European, North American, and regional actors.

highlights: Resource base remains under state pressure
Ports and corridors are arenas of external competition

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest regions continues to disrupt agriculture, transport, and state access to local resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and energy projects expand connectivity but raise concerns over debt exposure, procurement transparency, and strategic leverage.

highlights: State authority remains concentrated and externally supported
Mineral wealth is poorly converted into public capacity

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and political support strengthen regime survival while increasing foreign influence over security policy and access to extractive sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal mining and transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production remains vulnerable to armed-group taxation and cross-border smuggling, while weak roads limit formal state oversight.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a security-centered state
Sahel and Sudan spillovers narrow policy autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Crude exports and associated infrastructure remain central to public finance, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to international operators, price volatility, and opaque revenue management.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependency
frictionVectors.details: Instability linked to Sudan, Libya, and the wider Sahel increases reliance on foreign military and diplomatic partners while diverting resources from civilian infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest France's administration of Mayotte, making sovereignty and maritime jurisdiction a persistent bilateral fault line. The dispute also complicates migration management and access to surrounding waters.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external donors and partners for ports, energy, roads, and telecommunications. Limited domestic fiscal capacity reduces the government's leverage in negotiating investment terms.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-mineral bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, lithium, and other critical minerals attract Chinese, Western, and regional competition, while weak enforcement limits Kinshasa's ability to capture full value. Contract renegotiations and export controls remain major sovereignty tests.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed-group conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine state authority and disrupt trade corridors near Rwanda and Uganda. Regional mediation and external security involvement can constrain Kinshasa's operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains heavily dependent on oil exports and foreign technical capital, leaving public finances exposed to price volatility and contract asymmetries. Limited diversification weakens long-term control over national resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and other infrastructure expand connectivity but increase concerns over debt exposure and strategic dependence. The government retains formal control, yet financing conditions can narrow policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and local processing, but foreign traders and global manufacturers still capture substantial value. Climate stress and price volatility further constrain national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal security competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and offshore energy assets attract growing foreign investment and security partnerships. These ties improve resilience but require careful management to prevent excessive dependence on external capital and maritime capabilities.

highlights: Ports sit at a global chokepoint

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities, including U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other deployments. Base revenues strengthen the government but create exposure to great-power rivalry and reduce strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Control of port logistics and associated infrastructure is closely tied to foreign operators, financing, and regional trade flows. Debt obligations and competition with neighboring ports can limit Djibouti's ability to capture the full value of its geostrategic position.

highlights: Suez revenue and LNG assets remain strategic state levers
Gulf financing and IMF-linked reforms deepen external exposure

frictionVectors.title: Sovereign Asset Sales
frictionVectors.details: Privatization and Gulf-backed investment are supporting foreign-exchange liquidity but transferring greater influence over ports, real estate, and strategic firms to external actors.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to contested operating rules for a critical transboundary water system.

highlights: Hydrocarbon revenues still dominate fiscal sovereignty
Declining output raises dependence on foreign capital and infrastructure

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Depletion
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and weak diversification constrain state revenue, increasing reliance on international operators, service firms, and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Major public works and urban projects remain closely associated with Chinese construction and financing, creating long-term external leverage despite strong formal state control.

highlights: Strategic Red Sea geography strengthens bargaining power
Mining remains the principal channel for foreign resource access

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide scarce foreign exchange but expose the state to opaque contract terms, labor concerns, and dependence on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and competition around Red Sea ports increase pressure on Eritrea's coastline and transport infrastructure while limiting autonomous economic options.

highlights: Regional trade remains anchored to South African corridors
Sugar, textiles, and forestry provide limited but stable resource control

frictionVectors.title: South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Imports, logistics, electricity links, and investment are heavily tied to South Africa, constraining Mbabane's ability to pursue fully independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Agribusiness Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Competition over water-intensive agriculture and uneven infrastructure could intensify as climate variability affects sugar and forestry production.

highlights: GERD consolidates leverage over Nile energy and water politics
Debt restructuring and port access are central sovereignty tests

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable port access remains a major strategic issue, with arrangements involving Somaliland and regional actors drawing strong opposition from Somalia and scrutiny from Egypt.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external lenders constrain policy space, even as state-led power and transport projects expand domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: French Influence Reset
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is renegotiating long-standing French political, military, and commercial influence while seeking broader partnerships. The transition to elected rule has improved legitimacy but left uncertainty over the future role of foreign firms.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Control Concentration
frictionVectors.details: The state is asserting greater control over oil, manganese, and timber value chains, but fiscal dependence on extractive revenues and limited domestic processing remain significant vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for security coordination, trade access, and transport connectivity. This relationship stabilizes the country but constrains independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Resource Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring continue to threaten fisheries sovereignty and local livelihoods. Port and tourism infrastructure remain vulnerable to external financing and concessionary influence.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is degrading rivers, farmland, and public confidence in state resource governance. Efforts to formalize and police the sector face entrenched local interests and cross-border supply networks.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed stabilization limit policy space while increasing pressure to monetize minerals, oil, and critical-mineral prospects. Accra is seeking greater domestic value addition without losing investor access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite and Simandou iron-ore projects are attracting Chinese, Western, and regional capital, giving outside operators major influence over rail, port, and logistics infrastructure. Conakry is demanding more local processing and state participation but remains dependent on foreign expertise and finance.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Contract Risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining expansion to bolster legitimacy while delaying a full return to civilian rule. Political uncertainty raises the risk of abrupt regulatory changes, sanctions exposure, and uneven treatment of foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Cashew Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state finances exposed to foreign buyers, price volatility, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine Transit and Institutional Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and porous maritime borders sustain the country's exposure to transnational narcotics networks. Political instability and limited coast-guard capacity make external security assistance increasingly influential.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service demands and dependence on external lenders constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Major transport and energy projects remain exposed to foreign financing, contractors, and refinancing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing domestic control of the Mombasa corridor against competition from Tanzania and external commercial interests. Regional instability also raises the security costs of logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria for infrastructure, market access, and project financing. Delays and cost pressures could reduce Lesotho's bargaining leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Remittance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to shifts in external trade preferences and South African labor-market conditions. Foreign-owned textile operations provide employment but leave limited domestic control over value chains.

highlights: Ports and Minerals Under External Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining capital is central to Liberia's export earnings, but weak local processing and concession asymmetries limit domestic value capture. Infrastructure commitments remain vulnerable to commodity-price cycles and investor renegotiation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and surrounding logistics networks attract competing foreign commercial interests. Liberia is seeking investment while trying to preserve regulatory control and prevent strategic assets from becoming effectively concessioned.

highlights: Foreign Powers Shape the Security Map

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed networks continue to threaten unified management of production, export terminals, and public revenues. International energy firms retain influence because technical capacity and security remain unevenly controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and Mercenary Presence
frictionVectors.details: External military backing and foreign security contractors continue to affect territorial control and access to strategic infrastructure. This limits Libya's ability to convert hydrocarbon wealth into fully sovereign state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Value Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects attract substantial foreign capital but expose Madagascar to volatile prices and limited domestic processing. Fiscal and environmental disputes challenge the state's ability to secure a larger share of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Telecoms, and Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and regional powers are competing for influence over ports, telecommunications, and logistics infrastructure. Weak regulatory enforcement increases the risk that strategic assets develop without sufficient local ownership or transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, graphite and rare-earth projects, but limited domestic financing and technical capacity constrain its bargaining power. The government faces pressure to improve contract transparency and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Import Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Malawi remains dependent on costly routes through Mozambique and Tanzania for fuel, fertilizer and exports. Port congestion, transport costs and regional instability directly weaken sovereign economic resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing foreign mining companies for higher state participation, taxes and local processing. Disputes over operating terms risk investment delays and further strain relations with Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western leverage but increased exposure to opaque military and commercial arrangements. Persistent jihadist violence continues to threaten mining zones, transport corridors and state authority.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major fiscal and strategic upside, but revenue management, domestic content and cross-border coordination remain sensitive sovereignty issues. Delays or disputes could limit expected development gains.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Logistics Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania is expanding beyond iron ore, yet dependence on foreign operators, rail infrastructure and export terminals leaves the country vulnerable to external pricing and operational decisions. New green-energy and mining projects may deepen this dependency without stronger local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty Settlement
frictionVectors.details: The future status and administration of the Chagos Archipelago remain central to Mauritius's territorial sovereignty and maritime-resource claims. Any settlement must balance decolonization objectives with security arrangements surrounding Diego Garcia.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional capacity but remains exposed to global financial regulation, foreign investment cycles and reputational pressure on its offshore sector. Maintaining market access requires continued transparency and compliance reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of Western Sahara underpins major infrastructure, fisheries and renewable-energy plans, while the Polisario Front and Algeria continue to contest the territory's status. Legal and diplomatic challenges create persistent risk for foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale ports, railways, renewables and automotive projects strengthen Morocco's strategic autonomy but rely heavily on European, Gulf and Asian finance and technology. External partners therefore retain leverage over key infrastructure and industrial supply chains.

highlights: LNG restart remains the strategic prize
Cabo Delgado security still limits sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Gas development depends on multinational operators and external military support, leaving Maputo with constrained leverage over project timelines, revenues, and security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and local grievances continue to threaten energy infrastructure and displacement-affected communities despite regional and international counterinsurgency assistance.

highlights: Oil and uranium reshape the resource outlook

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Control
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries are attracting major foreign energy companies, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules, fiscal terms, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large external-backed hydrogen projects depend on imported technology, export corridors, and substantial land and water access, raising questions about domestic value capture.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic minerals
Pipeline access remains a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control and revenue from uranium and other mineral assets, increasing friction with established foreign operators and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Political hostility with Benin threatens the oil-export route and exposes Niger's dependence on neighboring infrastructure for monetizing new production.

highlights: Oil reform meets persistent production losses
Gas and domestic refining gain momentum

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and community grievances continue to reduce state capture of petroleum value and undermine investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Refining, gas, rail, and port projects rely heavily on foreign finance and contractors, limiting domestic control while expanding strategic exposure to Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Allegations of support for M23 continue to generate diplomatic pressure and concerns that regional security networks facilitate access to eastern Congolese mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Minerals Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model depends on external aid, investment, and mineral trading, leaving sovereign policy space vulnerable to sanctions, donor conditions, and supply-chain scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: JOINT DEVELOPMENT ZONE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe retains limited leverage over petroleum prospects in its joint zone with Nigeria, while exploration economics and licensing remain uncertain. External operators and Nigerian cooperation are essential to any future revenues.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA MARITIME SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and weak naval capacity constrain control of the country’s maritime resources. Port, connectivity, and security partnerships with outside powers can improve access while creating long-term dependence.

frictionVectors.title: SANGOMAR AND GTA GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production is strengthening state revenues but has intensified demands for contract review, local content, and greater national participation. Partnerships with foreign operators remain central to offshore development.

frictionVectors.title: FISCAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and costly energy infrastructure limit Dakar’s room to convert resource income into sovereign industrial capacity. Chinese, Gulf, European, and multilateral financing all carry influence over strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign fleets and investment for tuna processing and maritime activity, creating recurring concerns over licensing transparency and the capture of fisheries value abroad. Monitoring capacity remains a sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago balances security and infrastructure ties with India, China, Europe, and other partners. Port and maritime-surveillance cooperation can enhance resilience but risks narrowing strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and related rail and port infrastructure generate exports but leave the state exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over taxes and concession terms. Domestic processing remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold, rutile, bauxite, and other mineral projects attract Chinese and other foreign capital while raising concerns about land access, environmental damage, and revenue transparency. State capacity to enforce local-content commitments is uneven.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other external actors compete for influence over ports, security assistance, and logistics corridors. Fragmented authority, including disputes involving Somaliland, limits unified control of maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil and gas ambitions remain constrained by insecurity, federal-regional disputes, and limited regulatory capacity. Foreign exploration and security partners may provide essential capital while capturing substantial influence over future resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-security competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to South Africa's platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-mineral value chains. Pretoria is seeking local processing and strategic autonomy rather than simple raw-material exports.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail bottlenecks, and congested ports continue to reduce sovereign control over industrial supply chains. Private operators and foreign-linked investment are increasingly important to infrastructure recovery.

highlights: Oil remains the state’s survival lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-route dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on oil exports through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving revenue and production exposed to conflict, transit disruption, and external commercial leverage. The arrangement sharply limits independent control over the country’s principal resource.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign extraction networks
frictionVectors.details: Political elites, armed actors, and outside firms compete over oil, gold, and land while public institutions remain weak. Regional security actors can influence transport corridors, revenue flows, and peace implementation.

highlights: Gold and transit routes drive external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold economy and armed finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide critical financing for rival armed networks and attract regional and international intermediaries. The state has limited ability to regulate exports or convert mineral wealth into public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor contestation
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, Red Sea access, and overland corridors has become strategically valuable to outside powers and regional actors. Infrastructure damage and competing security patrons further erode national control.

highlights: Resource nationalism is becoming more commercial

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing foreign mining companies for greater state participation, domestic processing, and revenue transparency. This strengthens bargaining power but risks investment delays and arbitration pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and regional corridors
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional interests are competing around Dar es Salaam, Bagamoyo, railways, and links to landlocked neighbors. Infrastructure finance could expand national leverage while creating long-term dependency risks.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé and adjacent logistics networks give Togo outsized regional influence, but operations and expansion depend heavily on foreign capital and trade flows. This creates leverage for external commercial and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insurgency spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and trafficking pressure from the Sahel are testing Togo’s northern security infrastructure. Reliance on foreign training, intelligence, and border-support partnerships may expand as the threat persists.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Partnership
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to Tunisia's efforts to limit irregular migration, creating significant external leverage over domestic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Strain
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy output and recurring phosphate-sector disruptions increase dependence on imported fuel and external investment.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline to Tanzania remains central to Uganda's development strategy but faces Western political, legal, and financing opposition over environmental and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: China-West Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese infrastructure and energy partnerships compete with Western governance pressure, giving Kampala options but increasing exposure to geopolitical bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper remains dominated by foreign capital and technology, while Lusaka seeks greater taxation, local processing, and state participation without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Creditor Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral financing improve fiscal space but constrain policy autonomy and shape decisions on mining revenue and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Mineral Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is attracting Chinese and other foreign investment in lithium, platinum, gold, and diamonds, but weak transparency and limited domestic processing reduce sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Currency Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, currency instability, and infrastructure gaps increase reliance on external financiers and commodity-linked investment deals.
